title: Golf induced adaptions of executive functions and cognitive performance in context of dementia prevention - a randomized controlled trial
summary:
An increasing number of people experience memory problems as they grow older. These difficulties can significantly affect everyday life. Exercise and physical activity can help to maintain brain health and cognitive function. This has already been well studied for certain types of exercise, such as endurance and strength training. However, scientific evidence regarding the effects of golf on cognitive function remains limited. Golf is a sport that combines physical activity, coordination, concentration and social interaction. Therefore, this study aims to investigate whether playing golf—and more specifically a new golf training approach based on the Ball School concept—can help improve or maintain cognitive performance.
In this study, we investigate the new golf training concept based on the Ball School approach. One group will train according to this concept, a second group will receive a more traditional golf training and a third group will not participate in any additional training. We will compare the groups using various tests and assessments to determine whether the new training approach leads to greater improvements in cognitive performance, such as memory function, compared to the other conditions.
conditions: Healthy Elderly, People with cogntive decline (e.g.: subjective cognitive decline or mild cognitive impairment)

interventions.name: Golf training based on the Ball School approach (Participants attend training sessions twice a week over a period of 16 weeks. Each session lasts 120 minutes and consists of 60 minutes of training based on the Ball School approach, followed by 60 minutes of playing golf.)

Golf training based on the Ball School approach (Participants attend training sessions twice a week over a period of 16 weeks. Each session lasts 120 minutes and consists of 60 minutes of classic golf training, followed by 60 minutes of playing golf.)
Control group without additional training (Participants in the control group do not receive any additional training as part of the study.)

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Member of the University Golf Club Paderborn e.V.
Active golfer (defined as: having an official golf handicap or having played at least five rounds of golf in the past year (Hedegus et al., 2016)).
Exclusion criteria:
Medical contraindications to participation in a golf intervention
Acute injuries
